text: Given an integer array nums, find the subarray with the largest sum, and return its sum.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a subarray is a contiguous run of elements, and it can't be empty. So I must pick at least one number. And I only return the sum, not the start and end index. Is that right?
Yes. Non-empty, contiguous, and just the sum.

Okay. That non-empty part matters a lot. If every number is negative, the answer is still one of those numbers — it is not zero. For example, negative three, negative one, negative two should give negative one. I'll keep that in mind. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The array has up to ten to the fifth numbers, and each value is between negative ten thousand and ten thousand.

Got it. Up to a hundred thousand numbers, so I want one pass. The biggest possible sum is a hundred thousand times ten thousand, one billion, and the int limit is about two point one billion — so a plain int is enough. On the example, negative two, one, negative three, four, negative one, two, one, negative five, four, the best part is four, negative one, two, one, index three through six, for a sum of six. The point: it keeps the negative one inside, because its neighbors make up for it. The other two examples give one and twenty-three.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach tries every start index and grows the end with a running sum. That's quadratic — correct, but about three point seven seconds at a hundred thousand elements when I timed it. Too slow. This problem reminds me of a one-pass dynamic program, which is Kadane's algorithm. Look at the best subarray that ends right here. It has only two choices: extend the best one that ended one step before, or restart with just the current number. The answer is the best of these ends-here values over all indexes.

Here's the plan. One: keep cur-L, the best sum ending at the current number, and max-L, the best seen so far — max-L starts at the smallest int, cur-L at zero. Two: for each number, cur-L takes the larger of extend and restart. Three: max-L takes the larger of itself and cur-L, and I return it. One thing worth flagging — restart wins exactly when the past sum is negative, not when the current number is. Reset-on-negative fails on two, negative one, two: it gives two, the answer is three. Also, max-L must start at the smallest int, not zero — otherwise a single negative four returns zero, and that bug still passes all three official examples. Divide and conquer is n log n and more code; Kadane is linear time, constant space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Two ints — max-L at the smallest int, cur-L at zero — and one loop with two lines: cur-L becomes the max of extend and restart, then max-L becomes the max of itself and cur-L. Return max-L. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the order of those two lines. Updating cur-L first means max-L only ever sees a subarray that includes the current number, which keeps the empty subarray out. Swap them, and the first compare sees cur-L at zero — the empty subarray — so a single negative four returns zero again.

Let's dry-run the code with example one — expected six. The row where the decision happens is index three. Coming in, cur-L is negative two — the past can only hurt. Extend gives two, restart gives four, so I restart, exactly where the best subarray begins. From there cur-L never goes negative, so I keep extending, and max-L peaks at six on the window three to six. The later negative five drops cur-L to one, still positive, so no restart. Return six — that matches. Corner cases: all negative gives negative one, which is what the smallest-int start is for. A single element comes back as-is. Five, four, negative one, seven, eight never restarts and gives twenty-three. And a hundred thousand copies of ten thousand gives one billion, which fits in an int.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one pass, two max calls per number. Space is constant — two integers. There's no early exit, so it's always exactly n steps. At a hundred thousand elements it ran in about a quarter of a millisecond, versus nearly four seconds for the quadratic brute force. Oh, one more thing — I'd test this against the brute force on lots of small arrays. That's how the max-L-starts-at-zero bug shows up: it hides from the official examples but fails on every all-negative array.
Good. The follow-up asks for divide and conquer. How would that go?

I split the array in the middle. The best subarray is all in the left half, all in the right half, or crossing the middle. Left and right are recursive calls. For the crossing case, I take the best sum ending at the middle going left, plus the best sum starting right after it going right — one linear scan. Two half-size subproblems plus linear work gives n log n time, plus a logarithmic recursion stack. When I timed it at a hundred thousand elements, it took about one point six milliseconds, versus about a quarter of a millisecond for Kadane. So I'd ship Kadane, and keep divide and conquer as the follow-up answer.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed it as the best subarray that ends here — extend or restart — and showed the restart depends on the sign of the past sum, not the current number, with two, negative one, two. You explained why max-L must start at the smallest int — a single negative four would give zero — even though zero passes all the official examples. And you checked that an int is enough at one billion, then compared Kadane with divide and conquer on real numbers. Good work.
